item06.cause: When value equals minval, the Rust returns it without checking maxval, so inverted bounds like (5, 5, 3) give 5 instead of 3.

item10.cause: Rust requires every whitespace-separated token to be a whole number, so input like a final byte of 5x makes it error out where the C reads the 5 and prints the result.

item14.cause: the Rust reads the option’s argument before checking whether the option has one, so any flag without an argument, like -q, crashes.

item17.cause: The Rust starts the backward pass with the forward maximum instead of the last element, so [1, 2] gives 4 instead of 3.

item19.cause: After every event, the Rust gives a mention to every user it thinks is offline, so even a single direct mention like MESSAGE 10 id0 counts twice.

item20.cause: The Rust’s homemade number parser doesn’t skip leading spaces like strtol does, so " 12" prints an error instead of the totals.

item28.cause: Rust adds 0.5 and then also calls .round(), so it rounds twice, and 0.0 comes out as “North by east” instead of “North”.

item30.cause: Rust’s whitespace check also matches the array’s terminating zero byte, so stripping a zero-padded string like "ab\0\0" gives size 2 instead of 4.

item31.cause: The Rust’s buffer_append_n ignores its length argument, so appending the first 2 bytes of "hello" adds all 5.

item34.cause: Rust passes the same promoted value to the same libc functions and prints with the same formats, so there’s nothing to differetiate.

item38.cause: The Rust shifts each byte while it’s still 8 bits wide, so the shifts do nothing and (0, 1, 0, 0) gives 1 instead of 256.

item41.cause: Rust uses f32 instead of double, so for n = 8 the result loses precision and comes out as 61719996 instead of 61719994.
